notes: Replaced networkpolicy-ipblock-except-subtraction with networkpolicy-egress-ipblock-destination to avoid an answer implied by the field name. Replaced service-envvars-creation-order with service-envvars-namespace-scope to avoid repeating the ConfigMap environment snapshot fact in 4.3.

cards.statement: By default, a Pod in namespace apps with serviceAccountName unset uses the default ServiceAccount in namespace default.
cards.explanation: When serviceAccountName is unset, Kubernetes assigns the ServiceAccount named default in the Pod's own namespace. A Pod in apps uses apps' default ServiceAccount.
cards.misconception: Pods share the default namespace's default ServiceAccount when their serviceAccountName is unset.

cards.statement: The API server rejects changing serviceAccountName when you update an existing Pod.
cards.explanation: A Pod's serviceAccountName is fixed at creation. Create a replacement Pod to assign a different ServiceAccount.

cards.statement: A ServiceAccount's automountServiceAccountToken setting takes precedence over the Pod's setting.
cards.explanation: When both a Pod and its ServiceAccount set automountServiceAccountToken, the Pod's value controls automatic credential mounting for that Pod.
cards.misconception: The ServiceAccount's credential mounting choice overrides a conflicting choice on the Pod.

cards.statement: By default, the kubelet automatically rotates a projected ServiceAccount token before the token expires.
cards.explanation: The kubelet requests a replacement as the projected token approaches expiration. The application needs to reload the token file to use the replacement.

cards.statement: When runAsUser differs, the container's securityContext overrides the Pod's configured user ID.
cards.explanation: The runtime uses the container's runAsUser value when the Pod and container both specify it. The container-level value takes precedence for that container.

source.title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

cards.statement: With runAsNonRoot true, the kubelet automatically selects a nonzero UID for an image configured as root.
cards.explanation: runAsNonRoot makes the kubelet check the container's user and refuse startup if it would run as UID zero. The setting does not choose a replacement UID.
cards.misconception: runAsNonRoot assigns a non-root UID instead of validating the configured user.

cards.statement: With readOnlyRootFilesystem true, the runtime also makes a container's mounted volumes read-only.
cards.explanation: readOnlyRootFilesystem affects the container's root filesystem. Mounted volumes retain their own read/write settings, independent of that root filesystem setting.
cards.misconception: Making the root filesystem read-only also makes mounted volumes read-only.

source.title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

cards.statement: A Pod's securityContext supports capabilities settings that apply across its containers.
cards.explanation: Configure capabilities in each individual container's securityContext. PodSecurityContext does not provide a capabilities field for a Pod-wide setting.
cards.misconception: PodSecurityContext accepts capability changes that apply across the Pod's containers.

cards.statement: A runtime upgrade can change the syscall filter a Pod receives with seccompProfile.type set to RuntimeDefault.
cards.explanation: RuntimeDefault uses the container runtime's built-in profile. That profile can differ across runtime versions, so the field does not pin a fixed syscall allow-list.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

cards.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.36, with supporting kernels and runtimes, hostUsers false maps Pod UID zero to a non-root host UID.
cards.explanation: Setting hostUsers to false puts the Pod in a user namespace. The kubelet chooses a host mapping that lets root inside the container remain unprivileged on the host.

cards.statement: With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy, a new namespace's Pods permit incoming TCP traffic by default.
cards.explanation: Pods start open to incoming connections in a namespace that has no NetworkPolicies. Installing an enforcing plugin does not itself isolate them.

cards.statement: With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy, a policy with `policyTypes: [Ingress]` restricts its selected Pods' egress.
cards.explanation: A NetworkPolicy with policyTypes [Ingress] controls incoming connections. Its selection does not isolate the Pod for egress.
cards.misconception: Selecting a Pod for ingress isolation also restricts its outgoing connections.

cards.statement: With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy, a Pod's ingress allowance can come from either of two matching policies.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicies selecting a Pod combine their ingress allowances instead of intersecting them.

cards.statement: For new TCP connections, a NetworkPolicy-enforcing plugin lets destination ingress override blocked source egress.
cards.explanation: A new Pod-to-Pod connection needs permission for source egress and destination ingress. Permission at the destination does not override blocked source egress.
cards.misconception: Destination ingress permission overrides source egress isolation.

cards.statement: A NetworkPolicy's empty podSelector includes Pods with unrelated labels in that policy's namespace.
cards.explanation: An empty podSelector matches Pods throughout the policy's own namespace, regardless of their labels.

cards.statement: By default, a NetworkPolicy that defines egress rules and omits policyTypes applies to egress alone.
cards.explanation: Kubernetes defaults policyTypes to include Ingress and adds Egress when the NetworkPolicy defines egress rules.
cards.misconception: Egress rules alone make the inferred policyTypes egress-only.

cards.statement: A NetworkPolicy combines namespaceSelector and podSelector in one peer to select Pods within matching namespaces.
cards.explanation: A NetworkPolicy peer combines podSelector and namespaceSelector to select matching Pods in matching namespaces.

cards.statement: A NetworkPolicy's egress ipBlock matches the selected Pod's source address for outgoing connections.
cards.explanation: A NetworkPolicy egress rule's ipBlock matches destination IP addresses. The selected Pod is the connection source.
cards.misconception: An egress ipBlock filters the selected Pod's source IP.

cards.statement: A NetworkPolicy with endPort uses a named port as the start of its destination port range.
cards.explanation: A NetworkPolicy port range needs a numeric port value. The API server rejects endPort combined with a named port.
cards.misconception: A named port serves as the lower boundary of an endPort range.

cards.statement: With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy, ingress isolation still permits traffic from the Pod's own node.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy leaves connections from a Pod's resident node permitted, even when its ingress rules grant no access.

cards.statement: Changing a Pod's labels can move it into the backend set of an existing Service.
cards.explanation: The control plane watches for Pods matching the Service's selector and updates its backend set when their labels change.

cards.statement: When port and targetPort differ, clients connect to targetPort on the Service's cluster IP.
cards.explanation: Clients connect to the Service's port on its cluster IP. The Service forwards that traffic to the backend's targetPort.
cards.misconception: The targetPort is the client-facing port on the Service's cluster IP.

cards.statement: A Service's named targetPort reaches Pods that use different port numbers for the same port name.
cards.explanation: The Service resolves the named targetPort against each selected Pod's declared port. Matching port names can therefore refer to different numbers.

cards.statement: Kubernetes routes a selectorless Service via manual EndpointSlices matched by owner reference.
cards.explanation: An EndpointSlice's kubernetes.io/service-name label identifies the Service that uses its endpoints. An owner reference records ownership of the slice.
cards.misconception: An EndpointSlice's owner reference determines the Service that routes traffic through it.

cards.statement: With cluster DNS installed, a headless Service with a selector returns ready Pod IPs in DNS lookups by default.
cards.explanation: A headless Service's DNS records point to its backing Pods rather than a virtual cluster IP, so the client receives endpoint addresses.

cards.statement: With cluster DNS installed, a Pod's short Service name lookup searches across namespaces by default.
cards.explanation: A short Service name uses the querying Pod's namespace. To look up a Service in another namespace, include that namespace in the DNS name.
cards.misconception: A short Service name lookup searches Services throughout the cluster.

cards.statement: For application Services, the kubelet limits Service environment variable discovery to the Pod's namespace.
cards.explanation: The kubelet supplies environment variables for application Services in the Pod's own namespace. Services in another namespace do not contribute those variables.

cards.statement: For a Service backed by several Pods, `kubectl port-forward` can balance local connections across those Pods.
cards.explanation: kubectl port-forward selects one matching Pod and forwards the session to it. It does not use Service load balancing across the backend set.
cards.misconception: Forwarding through a Service load-balances connections across its backend Pods.

cards.statement: The EndpointSlice controller keeps an empty slice for a Service whose selector matches zero Pods.
cards.explanation: With zero selected Pods, the EndpointSlice controller preserves an empty placeholder slice. Its endpoints list contains no Pod addresses.

cards.statement: `kubectl port-forward` can reach an external database through a selectorless Service with manual EndpointSlices.
cards.explanation: The API server blocks proxying to endpoints that do not map to Pods. External database addresses in manual EndpointSlices therefore do not work with kubectl port-forward.
cards.misconception: Manually supplied EndpointSlices make an external Service backend available through kubectl port-forward.

cards.statement: The API server can accept valid Ingress objects before an administrator installs an Ingress controller.
cards.explanation: Creating an Ingress records routing configuration. An Ingress controller needs to implement that configuration before it affects traffic.

cards.statement: With a single default IngressClass, the API server assigns it when a new Ingress leaves its class unspecified.
cards.explanation: DefaultIngressClass admission assigns the single default class during Ingress creation. The new object's ingressClassName receives that class's name.

cards.statement: An Ingress's Secret reference lets you replace its configured certificate by editing the mutable Secret's data.
cards.explanation: An Ingress references a Secret that holds its certificate and private key. Updating that Secret replaces the configured certificate material.

source.title: Secrets: TLS Secrets and editing Secrets

cards.statement: For a host-specific Ingress rule, the controller uses both the request's host and path to select a backend.
cards.explanation: A host-specific Ingress rule needs a matching host and a matching path. A path match by itself does not satisfy both conditions.

cards.statement: An Ingress controller matches a request for `/Docs` against the Exact path `/docs` configured in that Ingress.
cards.explanation: Ingress Exact path matching is case-sensitive. A rule for /Docs does not match a request for /docs.
cards.misconception: Exact paths treat uppercase and lowercase characters as equivalent.

cards.statement: An Ingress controller treats the request path `/api-v2` as matching a Prefix path configured as `/api`.
cards.explanation: Ingress Prefix compares complete slash-separated elements; api-v2 is a different element from api.
cards.misconception: Prefix matches a substring inside the final path element.

cards.statement: A pathType of ImplementationSpecific lets an Ingress rule use regular-expression syntax defined by Kubernetes.
cards.explanation: ImplementationSpecific gives the selected Ingress controller control over path interpretation. Kubernetes leaves those matching semantics to that implementation.
cards.misconception: ImplementationSpecific supplies a portable regular-expression matching contract.

cards.statement: An Ingress controller prefers `/api/v2` over `/api` when both Prefix paths in one Ingress match a request.
cards.explanation: When Ingress paths match the same request, the longest path takes precedence; /api/v2 outranks /api.

cards.statement: In the Ingress specification, defaultBackend handles requests whose selected Service has zero Pods.
cards.explanation: Ingress defaultBackend covers unmatched requests. A matched rule keeps its backend selection even when that Service has zero Pods.
cards.misconception: defaultBackend supplies failover for a matched Service with zero Pods.

cards.statement: The standard Ingress TLS model sends the client's encrypted TLS session onward to the Service backend.
cards.explanation: Ingress TLS assumes termination at the Ingress entry point. The documented model sends plaintext traffic from there to the backend Service.
cards.misconception: Standard Ingress TLS forwards the encrypted client session to the backend for termination.
